qs.q: What specialized cells within the anterior pituitary gland primarily synthesize and secrete Growth Hormone?
qs.e: Somatotrophs within the anterior pituitary gland synthesize and secrete Growth Hormone. Lactotrophs secrete prolactin, and thyrotrophs produce TSH.
qs.s: Receptors and Growth Hormone Signaling: MCQs

qs.q: What rare condition can result from a TSH-secreting adenoma of the pituitary gland overstimulating the thyroid?
qs.e: Thyrotoxicosis can rarely be caused by TSH-secreting adenomas producing excess TSH and overstimulating the thyroid gland. Cushing's disease is caused by excess ACTH rather than TSH.
qs.s: Receptors and Growth Hormone Signaling: MCQs

qs.q: Which hypothalamic factor acts to inhibit the release of Growth Hormone from the anterior pituitary gland?
qs.e: Growth hormone release is stimulated by GHRH and inhibited by somatostatin. Corticotropin and dopamine serve different regulatory roles in the endocrine system.
qs.s: Receptors and Growth Hormone Signaling: MCQs

qs.q: What is the primary supportive cell type found within the neurohypophysis of the pituitary gland?
qs.e: The supporting cells of the neurohypophysis are termed pituicytes. Astrocytes are central nervous system glial cells, not neurohypophyseal specialists.

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The pituitary gland is a pea‑sized endocrine organ in the sella turcica that links the brain to the rest of the body. Its anterior and posterior lobes secrete distinct hormones that regulate growth, metabolism, reproduction, and water balance.

sections.p: The pituitary sits at the base of the skull, beneath the hypothalamus, and is the central hub of the endocrine system.
b: Two lobes: anterior (adenohypophysis) and posterior (neurohypophysis)
Connected to hypothalamus by the pituitary stalk

sections.p: It occupies the sella turcica of the sphenoid bone, protected by the diaphragma sellae.
b: Anterior lobe: glandular cells, derived from oral ectoderm
Posterior lobe: neural tissue, extension of hypothalamic axons

sections.p: Laterally bounded by cavernous sinuses, superiorly by the optic chiasm, and inferiorly by the sphenoid sinus.
b: Compression of optic chiasm → bitemporal hemianopia
Cavernous sinus involvement → ophthalmoplegia

sections.p: Arterial blood reaches the anterior lobe via the hypophyseal portal system; the posterior lobe receives direct arterial branches.
b: Superior hypophyseal arteries → portal veins → anterior lobe
Inferior hypophyseal arteries → posterior lobe

sections.p: The posterior lobe is innervated by hypothalamic neurosecretory axons; the anterior lobe lacks direct innervation.
b: ADH and oxytocin travel down axons to be released from posterior lobe
Anterior hormones released in response to hypothalamic releasing/inhibiting hormones

sections.p: The anterior pituitary secretes six tropic hormones; the posterior pituitary stores and releases ADH and oxytocin.
b: ACTH → adrenal cortisol
TSH → thyroid hormones
GH → growth & metabolism
LH/FSH → gonadal function
Prolactin → lactation
ADH → water reabsorption
Oxytocin → uterine contraction & milk ejection

sections.p: Disorders arise from tumours, vascular events, infection, or trauma, altering hormone output and causing systemic effects.
b: Pituitary adenoma (most common) – may cause excess hormone or mass effect
Sheehan syndrome – postpartum infarction, leads to panhypopituitarism
Pituitary apoplexy – hemorrhagic infarct, sudden headache, visual loss, adrenal crisis
Infections (TB, HIV) can involve the gland, especially in low‑resource settings

t.b: What structural abnormality is present? → Detect adenoma size, cavernous sinus invasion, apoplexy

t.a: Serum cortisol (8 am) + ACTH stimulation test
t.b: Is adrenal axis intact? → Low cortisol with blunted response indicates secondary adrenal insufficiency
Is hyperprolactinemia present? → Elevated level suggests stalk effect or prolactinoma

sections.p: Focus on hormone patterns, visual field testing, and emergency management of adrenal crisis.
b: Bitemporal hemianopia → lesion compressing optic chiasm
Low cortisol with normal ACTH → secondary adrenal insufficiency
Sudden severe headache + ophthalmoplegia → pituitary apoplexy

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe headache with vomiting and visual loss (possible pituitary apoplexy)
Acute adrenal crisis: hypotension, hyponatremia, hypoglycemia after pituitary injury

faq.q: Why does a prolactinoma cause loss of libido?
faq.a: Excess prolactin suppresses GnRH, lowering LH/FSH and testosterone/estrogen.

faq.q: Can a pituitary tumour cause diabetes insipidus?
faq.a: Only if the posterior lobe or stalk is damaged, reducing ADH release.

faq.q: What is the first step in managing suspected pituitary apoplexy?
faq.a: Stabilize airway, give high‑dose IV steroids, and arrange urgent MRI.
